Package io.webagent4j.browsercrawler.internal

Class PageStabilityWaiter

java.lang.Object
io.webagent4j.browsercrawler.internal.PageStabilityWaiter
public final class PageStabilityWaiter extends Object
Waits for a navigated page's DOM to stop changing, using IPage.waitForCondition(String, Duration) - a single, backend-natively-bounded call - rather than a Java-side polling loop that repeatedly calls IPage.evaluate(String).

Why not webagent4j-wait's WaitEngine: an earlier version of this class built a WaitPolicy.withStableFor(...) and drove it through WaitEngine.await(...), whose probe called page.evaluate(FINGERPRINT_SCRIPT) once per poll. WaitEngine only ever checks WaitBudget.expired() between probe calls - it has no way to interrupt a single probe call that is already in flight. evaluate() has no timeout of its own, so a poll that happened to land during a client-side navigation transition (a meta-refresh, a JS location.assign, or a router push mid-flight) could block the underlying Playwright call indefinitely: no exception, no timeout, no way back to Java until - if ever - the driver call itself returned. See BrowserCrawlerRobustnessIT's real-Playwright client-side-navigation-during-stability regression test for the reproduction this class resolves.

The fix: the entire "is the DOM stable" condition - fingerprint computation, change detection, and the stabilityWindow bookkeeping - is expressed as one JavaScript predicate and handed to the backend's own native timeout-aware polling primitive (IPage.waitForCondition(java.lang.String, java.time.Duration)). There is exactly one call from this class into the backend per stability wait, and that call - not a loop wrapped around it - is what the backend itself bounds to timeout: this is the architectural guarantee the whole class depends on, and it holds regardless of what happens to the page's execution context while the call is in flight. If the backend cannot honor this natively-bounded contract, IPage.waitForCondition(java.lang.String, java.time.Duration) fails explicitly (UnsupportedOperationException) rather than silently falling back to an unbounded loop.

Separately, and empirically: the Playwright adapter maps this onto Page.waitForFunction, which polls entirely driver-side. In the Playwright version currently pinned by this project (1.60.0), BrowserCrawlerRobustnessIT's client-side-navigation- during-stability regression exercises this call across a client-side navigation (a meta-refresh) that replaces the page's execution context mid-wait, and it completes rather than throwing "context destroyed" or hanging. That specific cross-navigation resilience is an observed behavior of the pinned Playwright version, proven by that test - not a documented, versioned contract of the Playwright Java API asserted here as a universal guarantee. This class's correctness does not rest on it: it rests only on the native-timeout guarantee described above.

awaitStable(io.webagent4j.browser.IPage, io.webagent4j.wait.WaitBudget, java.time.Duration) deliberately has no return value: IPage#waitForCondition itself carries none (see its contract - this caller never needed the fingerprint value, only "did it stabilize in time"), so there is nothing left to wrap in a result type. Success is returning normally; a timeout - whether the backend genuinely observed the condition never settle, or the shared budget was already exhausted before this method could even attempt a backend call - is always a ConditionTimeoutException, letting BrowserCrawler classify both the same way it classifies NavigationTimeoutException for navigation: by catching one typed exception, never by inspecting WaitBudget timing or a message.

The fingerprint is four parts: document.readyState; the total element count; the total count of href-bearing anchors and image-map areas (a[href], area[href]); and a bounded, order-stable digest of the first 2000 such links' href attributes, JSON.stringify-encoded (not delimiter-joined) so an href containing the delimiter cannot collide with a genuinely different sequence. 2000 is a generous, independently-chosen bound, not a guarantee of exact alignment with ObservationOptions.maxElements(2000)'s retained set: that bound caps the first 2000 *all-kind* semantic elements in document order (headings, buttons, forms, images, and more, not only links), so a link that is, say, the 1800th link on a page but the 2400th semantic element overall would be covered by this digest yet still missing from a truncated observation, and vice versa on a link-dense page. See docs/browser-crawler.md#stability for the exact, non-overclaiming contract.

The "stable since" timestamp inside the fingerprint predicate uses the page's own performance.now() - monotonic within one document/execution context, immune to system wall-clock changes - never Date.now(). A client-side full-document navigation replaces the execution context entirely, which resets both performance.now()'s own origin and the window-scoped state this predicate tracks its "since" timestamp on; that reset is intentional, not a bug to guard against - the newly-navigated document must establish its own stable interval from scratch, exactly as if it were a fresh page.

This still is not a general content-change detector (an anchor's visible text, a non-link element's content, or an href change past the digest boundary is not detected), and it still only ever reflects one observation point, never continued monitoring after stability is accepted - see docs/browser-crawler.md#stability.

    • awaitStable

      public void awaitStable(IPage page, WaitBudget budget, Duration stabilityWindow)
      Waits for page's DOM fingerprint to remain unchanged for stabilityWindow.
      Throws:
      ConditionTimeoutException - if the page does not stabilize within budget's remaining time - either because budget was already exhausted (by navigation itself consuming the whole shared budget) before this method could attempt a backend call, in which case the exception carries no cause, or because the backend's own bounded wait genuinely timed out, in which case the original ConditionTimeoutException thrown by IPage.waitForCondition(java.lang.String, java.time.Duration) propagates unchanged - this method never catches it, precisely so BrowserCrawler can preserve its typed provenance
